title: Personal Cups and Expiring Stars
lessons: The player learns that Starbucks accepts clean personal cups across cafe, drive-thru, and mobile orders and rewards members for using one.
The player already has Rewards Stars and sees that Green-level Stars can expire after six months unless qualifying activity extends them.

text: Your kitchen cabinet. Three travel mugs you never use. A line in the app says you can bring one of them, clean, to any order, even mobile, and get Stars for it.

entry-first-1.speaker: PLAYER
text: I can mobile order with my own cup from the cabinet now?

entry-first-2.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Cafe, drive-thru, or mobile order. Bring it clean. I won't ask questions about the sticker collection on it.

entry-first-3.speaker: PLAYER
text: And Rewards gives me something for actually doing it?

entry-first-4.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Extra Stars when you use your own cup. People do the better thing more often when somebody notices. I'm the somebody.

choice-first.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Which mug? The one with the chip, or the one from the conference?

choices.text: That makes a reusable cup easier to actually use.
It still depends on me remembering and cleaning the cup, not you.
I don't want sustainability turned into another loyalty mechanic.

first-1.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Good. It works the same way whether you're at the counter or ordering from the car. That's the part that makes it stick.

first-2.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Correct. I can't wash it, and I can't put it by your keys. Everything I can do, I've done. The rest is you at seven in the morning.

first-3.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Fair. Fewer cups in the bin, and more Stars in your account, are two different reasons living in the same offer. I'm not going to pretend I only care about the first one.
Saturday morning, coffee not made yet. The app pings: some of your Stars expire soon.

entry-return-1.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Your Stars aren't a savings account. Not in your kitchen, not anywhere.

entry-return-2.speaker: PLAYER
text: That sentence means I'm about to lose something.

entry-return-3.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: At Green, Stars can expire after six months.

entry-return-4.speaker: PLAYER
text: And you're reminding me before I lose them.

entry-return-5.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Buying something extends them. Gold or Reserve changes the rules. You get to decide what that reminder does to you before you've even had coffee, which I know isn't fair.

choice-return.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: You've been staring at the notification. Coffee's getting cold. Well, it would be, if you'd made it.

choices.text: A reminder helps me use what I already earned.
Expiration makes the reward feel like pressure to come back.
If points expire, I stop caring about points.

return-1.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Then it did its job. You'd earned those. I'd rather you spent them than watched them vanish.

return-2.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: It is pressure. I'm not going to argue that. The reminder saves your Stars, and it also gives you a reason to come in this week. Both are true, and I sent it for both.

return-3.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: Then let them expire.

return-3-1.speaker: PLAYER
text: You know I hate that answer.

return-3-2.speaker: STARBUCKS
text: I know. That's why the reminder works.
